Read the output

a05_output.Rmd

createTrajectories() returns a data frame and writes the same trajectory to Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv or Data/patientDataContinuous.csv in the study folder. Use column names rather than their positions when reading the result.

Columns

Column Meaning
subject_id The original patient identifier. Internal batching IDs are not exported.
state_label The selected clinical label, or START, EXIT or OUT OF COHORT.
state_start_date First date of the selected interval or discrete cycle.
state_end_date Last date of that interval or cycle, including this date.
time_in_cohort Years from trajectory start to this row’s start, calculated as elapsed days divided by 365.25.
seq_ordinal Consecutive occurrence number of the same label in that patient’s output rows. It resets when the label changes. It is not a cycle number.
state_id An identifier assigned to the label within the run. It is not a clinical concept ID or a cross-database key.
age Age in years at this row’s start, when a CDM demographic join is used. Otherwise NA.
gender_concept_id The CDM person’s recorded gender concept ID, when joined. Otherwise NA.
state_key Present only for merged studies. Identifies the original members of a state across runs with the same labels.

Dates are Date values in the returned R object and date strings in CSV. state_id may be character or numeric depending on the trajectory format. Treat it as an identifier, not as a quantity. For unmerged output, inspect its mapping with unique(trajectories[c("state_id", "state_label")]).

When reading a CSV, preserve patient identifiers as text:

trajectories <- read.csv(
  "MyStudy/Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv",
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = NULL
)
trajectories$state_start_date <- as.Date(trajectories$state_start_date)
trajectories$state_end_date <- as.Date(trajectories$state_end_date)
for (column in c("time_in_cohort", "seq_ordinal", "age", "gender_concept_id")) {
  trajectories[[column]] <- type.convert(trajectories[[column]], as.is = TRUE)
}

This keeps leading zeros, long identifiers and literal labels such as "NA". Only the known numeric columns are converted. For input already held in R, use character or integer64 values for large identifiers. The package cannot recover digits already rounded by numeric storage.

Observation boundaries and unresolved cycles

The first target-cohort interval supplies the trajectory’s start and end. An absorbing state can stop the trajectory earlier. With outOfCohortAllowed = TRUE, retained state records can extend its end, but not move its start earlier. The analyst is responsible for supplying valid observation bounds.

START marks the first date. EXIT marks the day after the retained follow-up endpoint. For discrete output, that is the end of the final cycle. Both markers have identical start and end dates. They do not contribute observed days and should not be counted as clinical states when estimating time spent in care.

OUT OF COHORT has a different meaning. It is a discrete cycle for which no state was selected. The cycle is still within the supplied observation period. Deleting such rows can make separated states look like adjacent observations. Choose how an analysis handles these gaps before estimating transitions.

Discrete dates are cycle dates

With lengthOfStay = 7, a cycle beginning January 1 ends January 7. The next begins January 8. If observation ends January 10, that final cycle contains three observed days. For non-marker rows, duration is as.integer(state_end_date - state_start_date) + 1.

One label represents the whole cycle according to the configured selection rule. Its start date is not necessarily the date that the selected event occurred. A selected death state stops generation after its cycle. The cycle is shortened to the actual death date only if the supplied trajectory boundary also ends there.

Separate death states can preserve whether a complication had occurred before death, if the analyst defines them that way. They do not preserve the exact within-week complication date. See the weekly example.

Continuous dates are interval dates

Continuous output keeps the selected interval endpoints, bounded by the target interval and absorbing-state rules. It does not invent state coverage in a gap or shift simultaneous records onto different days. Priority selection can split intervals. First and Overlap selection can retain overlapping intervals.

Two rows can therefore share a start date or cover some of the same days. A downstream model that needs one state at every instant must handle that explicitly. Summing overlapping interval lengths will overcount patient-time.

State membership

For merged studies, study$stateDictionary and Data/stateDictionary.rds describe each original or combined state:

Field Meaning
state_key Stable key built from the original member labels.
label Display label used in the trajectory.
members List of original state labels.
absorbing Whether selecting this state ends the trajectory.
allowedTransitions List of permitted destination keys.
state_id Run-local ID, added during generation.

Use members to inspect a combination. Do not split its display label or key. The dictionary does not include boundary or unresolved-gap markers. Unmerged studies do not produce this dictionary.

Files to keep

File Purpose
Settings/analysisSettings.rds Completed import and generation rules. For CDM studies it also contains the cohort JSON definitions used during import.
Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv or Data/patientDataContinuous.csv Patient trajectories.
Data/importedDataCleaned_*.csv Intervals used as input to trajectory generation. The filename suffix identifies the target definition.
Data/sourceIntervals.rds Merged studies only. Cleaned intervals before overlapping states were combined.
Data/stateDictionary.rds Merged studies only. Membership and resolved state rules.

The interval files have already been cleaned. Observation limits and mandatory state requirements have been applied, and overlapping records of the same state have been combined. They are not a copy of every original database row. In merged studies, use sourceIntervals.rds to inspect the original state labels before composition.

The version-4 settings file stores import and generation separately because some choices can be supplied at generation time. For example, the cycle length is under settings$generation$lengthOfStay. Clinical rules remain the analyst’s responsibility even though their execution settings are saved.

When sharing a study, copy Settings, not Data. The settings file contains no patient records or database connection. It does include study-specific cohort definitions, which should be reviewed before sharing.

Handing the result to an analysis package

Pass the trajectory together with the settings and, for merged studies, the state dictionary. An analysis needs to know the cycle length, boundary-marker meaning, absorbing states and state membership. Do not infer these from label spelling or from the order of numeric IDs.

Cohort2Trajectory constructs histories. It does not estimate transition probabilities, survival effects, costs or cost-effectiveness. Check that the downstream package accepts the current column names and identifiers, treats observation end separately from a clinical outcome, and handles shortened cycles as intended. Exact event-time analyses also need the relevant state intervals rather than dates inferred from weekly labels.
